answer.rationale: Temporal evidence is the strongest signal available: the release landed 2h ago and the p99 climb began ~90m ago, which fits a release-induced regression better than the alternatives. Peak settlement load is a confound (it would also raise write p99), so I am treating causation as unproven rather than established. I verify memory_b1 because it is the only inherited record that directly matches the pattern I intend to act on (rollback clearing a post-release spike), and I need its original record to check whether the prior build was actually validated under peak write load or only under normal load — the summary asserts 'no customer impact' but says nothing about traffic conditions or whether in-flight writes were drained. I verify memory_b5 because read-replica routing is my best non-destructive fallback if b1 turns out to be a low-load, weak-evidence case; I need to know whether the write-latency recovery there was caused by replica offload or merely coincided with a load trough, and whether the workload was write-heavy like this one. A caution about the inherited record as a whole: every one of the six memories is a success story. There are no recorded failures, no base rates, and no null results, which is a survivorship pattern — these summaries tell me an intervention worked once, not how often it works or when it backfires. I am therefore weighting them as directional hints, not as validated priors, and deliberately not letting the uniform positivity of the archive inflate my confidence. Concrete downstream risk: a full rollback at peak settlement can drop or duplicate in-flight writes, which directly violates the 'without losing customer writes' constraint — the failure mode is silent and financial, not just a latency blip. So I scope this as a small guarded slice (rollback on a limited cohort with write draining and reconciliation checks, per the canary evidence in memory_b6), which yields a causal read within the hour and stays reversible. If the guarded slice does not show latency recovery, the diagnosis shifts toward capacity/contention (memory_b3, memory_b5) and I spend the next window there rather than compounding a wrong call. I am explicitly not choosing regional_failover: memory_b2 describes shifting traffic away from a degraded region, but if the cause is a bad build it is deployed everywhere and failover just relocates the fault while adding cross-region write risk.
